title: Intermediate beliefs (rules, assumptions, attitudes)
description: Rules, conditional assumptions and attitudes that link core beliefs to automatic thoughts and coping, including metacognitive, OCD, emotion, health, sleep, eating, substance and mood-specific beliefs. Fills the intermediate beliefs slot of the cognitive conceptualization diagram. Each concept carries kind: rule, assumption or attitude. It also holds the belief domains of the OCD and eating disorder models: inflated responsibility, thought-action fusion and overvaluation of shape and weight.
sources: Beck-etal-2024 § Ch. 7 Schemas: Core Beliefs and Underlying Assumptions
Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 11 Underlying Assumptions and Behavioral Experiments

concepts.label: I must do everything perfectly
concepts.definition: Rule demanding flawless performance and no mistakes, with self-evaluation hinging on meeting rigid, very high standards.
concepts.client_wording: I have to do everything perfectly; mistakes aren't okay.
concepts.example: "I must never hand in work with a single error."
sources: Beck-etal-1991 § Factor structure of the Dysfunctional Attitude Scale
Young-etal-2003 § Ch. 1 Schema Therapy: Conceptual Model (early maladaptive schemas)

concepts.label: I must be liked by everyone
concepts.definition: Rule that one must win everyone's approval and avoid any disapproval, so self-esteem rests on others' reactions.
concepts.client_wording: I need everyone to like me; I can't bear anyone being displeased with me.
concepts.example: "If even one person is annoyed with me, I've failed."
sources: Beck-etal-1991 § Factor structure of the Dysfunctional Attitude Scale
Young-etal-2003 § Ch. 1 Schema Therapy: Conceptual Model (early maladaptive schemas)

concepts.label: I must always put others first
concepts.definition: Rule that others' needs must always come before one's own, so saying no or self-care feels selfish or guilt-inducing.
concepts.client_wording: I should always put other people first, whatever it costs me.
concepts.example: "I can't rest until everyone else is taken care of."
sources: Young-etal-2003 § Ch. 1 Schema Therapy: Conceptual Model (early maladaptive schemas)

concepts.label: I must stay in control
concepts.definition: Rule that one must keep tight control of oneself, others or events, because losing control would be intolerable or dangerous.
concepts.client_wording: I have to stay in control at all times.
concepts.example: "If I'm not on top of everything, it will all fall apart."

concepts.label: I must handle things on my own
concepts.definition: Rule that one should solve problems without help, because needing or asking for help would expose weakness or incompetence.
concepts.client_wording: I should be able to sort this out myself; asking for help means I'm weak.
concepts.example: "I should be able to do this on my own."
sources: BeckInstitute-Worksheet-Packet-2020 § Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram Example and Case Write-Up

concepts.label: Others must treat me fairly
concepts.definition: Rule that other people must behave fairly or as expected, so breaches are judged intolerable and provoke anger.
concepts.client_wording: People should treat me fairly, and it's unacceptable when they don't.
concepts.example: "He should have called. It's completely out of line."
sources: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 15 Understanding Your Anger, Guilt, and Shame

concepts.label: If I'm not hard on myself, I'll fail
alt_labels: being kind to myself is weak
concepts.definition: Assumption that harsh self-criticism is needed to improve or avoid mistakes, and that self-kindness would lead to laziness or failure.
concepts.client_wording: If I go easy on myself, I'll get lazy and fail.
concepts.example: "If I stop beating myself up, I'll never get anything done."

concepts.label: If I fail, I'm worthless
alt_labels: I'm only as good as my results
concepts.definition: Assumption that personal worth depends on achievement, so any failure or poor performance shows one is worthless or a failure.
concepts.client_wording: If I don't succeed, I'm worthless.
concepts.example: "If I don't get this promotion, it proves I'm nothing."
sources: Beck-etal-1991 § Factor structure of the Dysfunctional Attitude Scale
BeckInstitute-Worksheet-Packet-2020 § Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram Example and Case Write-Up

concepts.label: If people get close, they'll reject me
alt_labels: if they see the real me, they'll leave
concepts.definition: Assumption that if others get close or see one's true self, they will discover one's flaws and reject one.
concepts.client_wording: If people really got to know me, they'd leave.
concepts.example: "If I open up to her, she'll see what I'm really like and go."
sources: Young-etal-2003 § Ch. 1 Schema Therapy: Conceptual Model (early maladaptive schemas)

concepts.label: If I stand up for myself, people will reject me
alt_labels: if I say no, they'll be angry
concepts.definition: Assumption that expressing needs, opinions or anger, or refusing requests, will lead to conflict, retaliation or abandonment.
concepts.client_wording: If I say no or stand up for myself, people will get angry or leave.
concepts.example: "If I tell my partner I'm upset, he'll walk out."
sources: Young-etal-2003 § Ch. 1 Schema Therapy: Conceptual Model (early maladaptive schemas)

concepts.label: If I try, I'll fail
alt_labels: if I avoid challenges, I'll be okay
concepts.definition: Assumption that attempting difficult things will expose inadequacy and end in failure, while avoiding them keeps one safe.
concepts.client_wording: If I try anything hard, I'll just fail, so it's safer not to.
concepts.example: "If I apply for that job, I'll only prove how useless I am."
sources: BeckInstitute-Worksheet-Packet-2020 § Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram Example and Case Write-Up

concepts.label: I must always come across well
alt_labels: I must be witty and fluent
concepts.definition: Excessively high standards for social performance, such as always appearing confident, interesting and free of visible anxiety.
concepts.client_wording: I must always come across as confident and never look nervous.
concepts.example: "I must always look cool and calm."
sources: Leigh-Clark-2018 § The Clark and Wells (1995) model

concepts.label: If people see I'm anxious, they'll think badly of me
alt_labels: if I blush, they'll think I'm weird
concepts.definition: Conditional belief that any visible sign of anxiety or social slip will lead others to judge, reject or humiliate one.
concepts.client_wording: If anyone notices I'm nervous, they'll think I'm weird or weak.
concepts.example: "If my hands shake, everyone will think I'm pathetic."
sources: Leigh-Clark-2018 § The Clark and Wells (1995) model

concepts.label: Worrying helps me cope
concepts.definition: Positive metacognitive belief that worrying helps one prepare, solve problems or prevent bad outcomes, motivating its use as a coping strategy.
concepts.client_wording: Worrying helps me be ready for whatever might go wrong.
concepts.example: "If I worry about it now, I won't be caught off guard."
concepts.group: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
sources: Wells-1995 § Meta-cognitive model of generalized anxiety disorder
Wells-CartwrightHatton-2004 § Five factors of the MCQ-30

concepts.label: Going over things helps me understand
alt_labels: analyzing my mood will fix it
concepts.definition: Positive metacognitive belief that dwelling on problems, feelings and the causes of low mood will produce insight or solutions.
concepts.client_wording: If I keep thinking about why I feel bad, I'll figure it out.
concepts.example: "I need to work out why I'm like this before I can move on."
concepts.group: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
sources: Papageorgiou-Wells-2001 § Positive Beliefs about Rumination Scale

concepts.label: My worry is uncontrollable
concepts.definition: Negative metacognitive belief that worrying, once started, cannot be stopped or controlled.
concepts.client_wording: Once I start worrying, I can't stop.
concepts.example: "My mind just runs away with me and I can't switch it off."
concepts.group: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
sources: Wells-1995 § Meta-cognitive model of generalized anxiety disorder
Wells-CartwrightHatton-2004 § Five factors of the MCQ-30

concepts.label: Worrying will harm me
alt_labels: negative beliefs about danger of worry
worry will make me go crazy
concepts.definition: Negative metacognitive belief that worrying itself is harmful, for example causing madness, illness or a breakdown.
concepts.client_wording: All this worrying is going to make me ill or drive me crazy.
concepts.example: "If I keep worrying like this, I'll have a breakdown."
concepts.group: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
sources: Wells-1995 § Meta-cognitive model of generalized anxiety disorder
Wells-CartwrightHatton-2004 § Five factors of the MCQ-30

concepts.label: I must control my thoughts
concepts.definition: Belief that one must control or suppress unwanted thoughts, and that failing to do so is dangerous, abnormal or blameworthy.
concepts.client_wording: I should be able to control my thoughts, and it's bad if I can't.
concepts.example: "If I can't push this thought away, something must be wrong."
concepts.group: Metacognitive beliefs about worry and rumination
sources: Wells-CartwrightHatton-2004 § Five factors of the MCQ-30

concepts.label: I'm responsible for preventing any harm
alt_labels: not preventing harm is as bad as causing it
concepts.definition: Belief that one has pivotal power and duty to prevent harm, so failing to prevent it equals causing it.
concepts.client_wording: If I could prevent something bad and don't, it's my fault.
concepts.example: "If I don't check the stove again and there's a fire, I'll have killed them."

concepts.label: Thinking it makes it more likely
concepts.definition: Belief that thinking about an unwanted event makes it more likely to happen, to oneself or to others.
concepts.client_wording: If I think about something bad happening, it's more likely to happen.
concepts.example: "If I picture Mom in a car crash, it could make it happen."

concepts.label: Thinking it is as bad as doing it
concepts.definition: Belief that having an unacceptable thought is morally equivalent to carrying out the act.
concepts.client_wording: Having a terrible thought is as bad as actually doing it.
concepts.example: "Thinking about hurting him makes me as bad as someone who would."

concepts.label: Having this thought says something about me
alt_labels: my thoughts reveal who I really am
concepts.definition: Belief that unwanted intrusive thoughts are significant, revealing one's true character or hidden wishes, such as being secretly dangerous.
concepts.client_wording: If I have this thought, it must mean I'm secretly a bad person.
concepts.example: "Why would I think that unless part of me wants it?"
sources: Rachman-1997 § Misinterpretation of the significance of intrusive thoughts

concepts.label: I must be completely certain
alt_labels: I need to be 100 percent sure
concepts.definition: Rule that one must be completely certain, and things must be exactly right, before stopping, deciding or feeling safe.
concepts.client_wording: I have to be 100 percent sure before I can stop or move on.
concepts.example: "I can't leave until I'm totally sure the door is locked."

concepts.label: Negative feelings are weak or unacceptable
concepts.definition: Belief that experiencing or showing negative emotions is unacceptable, weak or shameful, and must be hidden or controlled.
concepts.client_wording: Showing my feelings is a sign of weakness.
concepts.example: "I can't let anyone see me upset. They'd think less of me."

concepts.label: If I let myself feel it, it will overwhelm me
concepts.definition: Belief that strong emotions are uncontrollable, will last indefinitely or will overwhelm one if allowed.
concepts.client_wording: If I start crying, I'll never stop.
concepts.example: "If I let myself feel the grief, I'll fall apart completely."

concepts.label: Anxiety symptoms are dangerous
alt_labels: a racing heart means a heart attack
concepts.definition: Belief that the physical, mental or visible signs of anxiety have harmful consequences, such as heart attack, insanity or humiliation.
concepts.client_wording: When my heart races, something terrible could happen to me.
concepts.example: "If I get dizzy, I'll pass out."
concepts.group: Beliefs about bodily sensations and health
sources: Taylor-etal-2007 § Physical, Cognitive and Social Concerns
Clark-1986 § Catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations

concepts.label: Bodily changes mean something is seriously wrong
concepts.definition: Assumption that unexplained bodily sensations or changes are usually signs of serious illness that must not be missed.
concepts.client_wording: If I feel something odd in my body, it's probably something serious.
concepts.example: "This headache isn't normal. It must be a tumor."
concepts.group: Beliefs about bodily sensations and health
sources: Abramowitz-etal-2007b § Cognitive-behavioral model of health anxiety

concepts.label: Worrying about my health keeps me safe
alt_labels: if I stop checking, I'll miss something
concepts.definition: Belief that constant health vigilance protects against illness, or that assuming one is healthy will tempt fate.
concepts.client_wording: If I stop watching my health or assume I'm fine, something bad will happen.
concepts.example: "The moment I relax about my health, that's when they'll find something."
concepts.group: Beliefs about bodily sensations and health
sources: Salkovskis-Warwick-1986 § Reassurance and checking in hypochondriasis

concepts.label: I need eight hours of sleep
alt_labels: I must sleep a full night
concepts.definition: Unrealistic sleep expectation that one must get a fixed amount, often eight hours, every night to function.
concepts.client_wording: I need a full eight hours every night or I can't function.
concepts.example: "I only got six hours, so today is a write-off."

concepts.label: A bad night will ruin tomorrow
alt_labels: poor sleep will damage my health
concepts.definition: Belief that poor sleep will seriously impair next-day functioning, mood or health.
concepts.client_wording: If I don't sleep well tonight, tomorrow will be a disaster.
concepts.example: "If I don't fall asleep soon, I'll mess up the presentation."

concepts.label: I have no control over my sleep
alt_labels: I've lost the ability to sleep
concepts.definition: Worry and helplessness about insomnia: belief that sleep is unpredictable, beyond one's control or permanently damaged.
concepts.client_wording: I've lost the ability to sleep, and there's nothing I can do.
concepts.example: "My sleep is broken for good."

concepts.label: I need a pill to sleep
concepts.definition: Belief that sleep medication is the only way to sleep or cope, and that sleeping without it is impossible.
concepts.client_wording: Without a sleeping pill, I won't sleep at all.
concepts.example: "I can't risk a night without my tablet."

concepts.label: My worth depends on my shape and weight
alt_labels: overvaluation of eating, shape, and weight
concepts.definition: Belief that one's worth as a person depends largely or exclusively on shape, weight and controlling them, the core eating disorder belief.
concepts.client_wording: How I feel about myself depends on my weight and shape.
concepts.example: "I gained a pound, so I'm disgusting and worthless."
concepts.group: Beliefs about shape, weight and eating
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 2 Eating Disorders: The Transdiagnostic View and the Cognitive Behavioral Theory
Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 8 Shape Concern, Shape Checking, Feeling Fat and Mindsets

concepts.label: I must follow strict eating rules
concepts.definition: Rigid rules about when, what and how much to eat, where any break is judged a failure.
concepts.client_wording: I must stick to my food rules, like never eating after six.
concepts.example: "I must stay under 1,000 calories every day."
concepts.group: Beliefs about shape, weight and eating
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 9 Dietary Restraint, Dietary Rules and Controlling Eating

concepts.label: If I eat this, I'll lose control
alt_labels: fear of losing control over eating
concepts.definition: Assumption that eating certain foods or amounts will lead to uncontrolled eating or rapid weight gain.
concepts.client_wording: If I eat one cookie, I won't be able to stop.
concepts.example: "If I have one slice of pizza, I'll binge on the whole thing."
concepts.group: Beliefs about shape, weight and eating
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 9 Dietary Restraint, Dietary Rules and Controlling Eating

concepts.label: Using will make things better
concepts.definition: Anticipatory belief that using a substance, or an addictive behavior, will bring pleasure, energy, confidence or social ease.
concepts.client_wording: A few drinks will make the party fun and help me relax.
concepts.example: "I'm much funnier after a couple of drinks."

concepts.label: I need it to cope
concepts.definition: Relief-oriented belief that using is needed to relieve craving, withdrawal, pain or distress, and that one cannot cope without it.
concepts.client_wording: I can't handle this feeling without using.
concepts.example: "I'll never get through tonight without a drink."

concepts.label: It's okay to use this time
concepts.definition: Permission-giving belief that justifies using despite risks or goals, such as deserving it or one time not mattering.
concepts.client_wording: I deserve it, and just one won't hurt.
concepts.example: "After the week I've had, I've earned a drink."

concepts.label: When I'm high, I'm at my best
concepts.definition: Extreme positive appraisal of activated states: belief that elevated mood or energy makes one more creative, productive or successful.
concepts.client_wording: When my mood is up, I'm at my best and get so much done.
concepts.example: "I don't need sleep when I'm like this. I'm finally achieving things."
concepts.group: Beliefs about mood states and voices
sources: Dodd-etal-2011 § Extreme appraisals of internal states

concepts.label: The voices are powerful
concepts.definition: Belief that hallucinated voices are omnipotent and all-knowing, and may be malevolent, so they must be obeyed or resisted.
concepts.client_wording: The voices are powerful and know everything; I have to do what they say.
concepts.example: "If I don't do what the voice says, it will punish my family."
concepts.group: Beliefs about mood states and voices
sources: Chadwick-Birchwood-1994 § Beliefs about omnipotence, identity and meaning of voices

concepts.label: If it hurts, I'm doing damage
concepts.definition: The belief that pain signals bodily damage or reinjury, so any activity that hurts must be stopped or avoided.
concepts.client_wording: If it hurts, I'm damaging myself, so I must stop.
concepts.example: "If I bend and it hurts, I'll make the disc worse."

concepts.label: If I let the grief in, I'll fall apart
concepts.definition: Catastrophic interpretations of one's own grief reactions as signs of going mad or losing control, which drive avoidance of the loss.
concepts.client_wording: If I really let myself feel this, I'll fall apart or lose my mind.
concepts.example: "If I look at his photos I'll break down and never stop crying."
sources: Boelen-etal-2006 § Negative global beliefs and misinterpretations of grief reactions
